title: A half-open breaker that starts over on a failed probe keeps probing a dead dependency
summary: A half-open circuit breaker reopens on a probe that fails, and the wait starts again. A developer makes a failed probe start the probes over instead, so that one bad probe does not condemn a dependency on its way back and the breaker closes on the permitted number of successes in a row; the contract changes in four rows, from reopening to a half-open state with its metrics reset, and the test of a failed probe is updated to say so. Every safety invariant holds. The liveness check finds the run in which the dependency stays down: the breaker opens, waits, probes, and from the first failed probe on it is half-open forever, probing a dead dependency at the rate of its probe cap, with no wait ever again. The property that fails is the one that says a dependency which stays down gets the wait between its rounds of probes.

change.description: In the HALF_OPEN state, answer a failed probe with a transition that stays HALF_OPEN and carries RESET_METRICS, instead of reopening with START_WAIT, with the reasoning in a comment: one failed probe does not condemn a dependency on its way back, the probes start over, and the breaker closes once the permitted number in a row have succeeded. The contract of `CircuitBreaker#decide` is regenerated: the four rows of a failed probe, whatever the window and the threshold say, go from reopening to a reset. The test of a failed probe expects the reset; the class comment describes the new rule.

risk: The half-open state is a limited experiment: a few calls, then a decision, and if the decision is to reopen, a wait before the next experiment. A failed probe that starts the probes over removes the decision, and with it the wait. A dependency that is down for good then receives probes for as long as it is down, as many at a time as the probe cap allows, each one a real call that takes the full timeout to fail; the breaker has become a rate limiter at the probe cap, and the dependency never gets the quiet period that a breaker exists to give it. The window of the half-open state is reset on each failure, so the failure rate never reaches the threshold, and the rule that reopens the breaker when it does is never reached. No safety invariant sees it: the probes are limited, nothing is let through before a wait, the breaker never closes early. The tests pass, because the developer updated the one that expected a failed probe to reopen, and the comment reads as a reasonable intention: be patient with a dependency that is recovering.
explanation: Under the first configuration TLC explores every interleaving within the model's bounds, 94 states, and every safety invariant holds. Under the second, the fairness conditions of `LiveSpec`, the third property fails: `ADeadDependencyIsLeftAlone`, which says that once the dependency is down for good, the breaker opens again and again, so that no round of probes is followed by another without a wait. TLC shows the run. The dependency is down; two calls fail with a third in flight, and the window opens the breaker, dropping the third call as stale; the wait elapses over two ticks; a call is let through as the first probe, in a fresh generation; the stale call completes, dropped; the probe fails, and the rule resets the metrics and stays half-open; two more probes are let through, and one fails with the other in flight, which the reset drops as stale. From there the run is a cycle of six steps that the system never leaves: probes let through, probes failing, resets, and in no state of it is the breaker open. The run respects every fairness condition: every call completes, and the clock, with no wait to count down, has nothing to tick. The first two properties hold of this rule, since an open breaker still probes again and a dependency that comes back still closes it; it took the third, written for the dependency that does not come back, to see this run.
resolution: Keep the reopening: a failed probe is the half-open state's answer, and the wait that follows is what the dependency needs. If one failed probe is too harsh a verdict, judge the probes together by their failure rate, as example 076 does and as Resilience4j does, which keeps the decision and the wait; the liveness check confirms that rule under the same fairness. Then keep the three liveness properties in the build: each is written for a different fate of the dependency, and this change was invisible to the two written for one that comes back.
notes: The circuit-breaker model (`apps/crosscut/spec`) checks the breaker with the component that owns it for its invariants and, under fairness, for three liveness properties, each written for a different fate of the dependency behind it. A rule can keep every invariant and still fail one of them.
Probes a dead dependency forever with no wait between the rounds. Every invariant holds; only the liveness property for a dead dependency sees it.
provenance: Constructed from a consecutive-successes rule for the half-open state, as some breaker libraries offer it, applied without the reopening that keeps it bounded; the property it breaks is the one that gives a dead dependency its wait.

references.title: Resilience4j, CircuitBreaker: the OPEN, HALF_OPEN and CLOSED states, waitDurationInOpenState and permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState
Nygard, Release It! (the circuit breaker pattern)
Lamport, Specifying Systems, chapter 8: liveness and fairness, and section 14.3.5, checking liveness with TLC
